questions.question: Explain why relations between Japan and the United States broke down by 1941.
questions.expected_answer: Japan lacked oil and raw materials and its military leaders sought an Asian empire: Manchuria 1931 (leaving the League in 1933), full-scale war in China from 1937 including the Nanjing Massacre, the Tripartite Pact of September 1940 and occupation of French Indochina in 1940-41. The United States supported China, froze Japanese assets in July 1941 and stopped oil exports, about 80 per cent of Japan's oil. It demanded withdrawal from China and Indochina (Hull Note, November 1941). Tojo's government chose war to seize South-East Asian resources.

questions.question: Describe the attack on Pearl Harbour and assess its success for Japan.
questions.expected_answer: On Sunday 7 December 1941, six carriers under Nagumo launched 353 aircraft in two waves from 7:55 a.m. All eight battleships were damaged and four sunk (Arizona exploded, 1 177 dead); about 188 aircraft were destroyed; 2 403 Americans died. Japan lost 29 aircraft. It was a tactical success, but the carriers were at sea, fuel tanks and repair yards were spared, most ships were repaired, and it united America for war, making it a strategic mistake.

questions.question: Explain the consequences of Pearl Harbour for the course of World War II.
questions.expected_answer: The United States declared war on Japan on 8 December after Roosevelt's infamy speech (Congress voted 82-0 and 388-1); Germany and Italy declared war on the US on 11 December, making the war global; the Allies adopted Germany first. American industry produced vast amounts of weapons. Japan advanced for six months (Hong Kong, Singapore 15 February 1942, Philippines, Dutch East Indies) until losing four carriers at Midway in June 1942, after which it was on the defensive. Japanese Americans were interned.
